title: American Vlogger Tries Kulfi for the First Time in Amritsar, Gives It a Perfect 10
excerpt: Content creator AJ Elizarde discovers India's dense, slow-cooked frozen dessert at a street stall in Punjab and can't stop praising its nutty, milky complexity.
body:
• American content creator AJ Elizarde tried kulfi for the first time while exploring Amritsar, paying Rs 40 for a serving from a local vendor.
  • He described the Indian frozen dessert as "super sweet, super salty, kind of nutty and milky" and gave it a perfect 10 out of 10 score.
  • The Instagram video went viral, with Indian viewers sharing recommendations for rabdi kulfi and other regional variations.
  • Kulfi differs from Western ice cream — it is denser, creamier and is traditionally made by slow-cooking sweetened milk without churning.

AJ Elizarde, an American content creator exploring India, tried kulfi for the first time at a street vendor's stall in Amritsar — and his unfiltered reaction has since gone viral on Instagram. The vlogger paid Rs 40 for a serving of Punjabi kulfi and rated it a perfect 10 out of 10, according to NDTV Food.

The First Bite

In the video, Elizarde approaches a local kulfi vendor while walking through Amritsar. After asking what the vendor is selling and ordering a serving, he turns to his camera to introduce the dessert to his followers. "Alright guys, we're gonna be trying this cone-looking popsicle here. I guess they call it kulfi," he says, clearly unfamiliar with the treat.

His first impression captures what many first-time tasters experience — a combination of flavors that doesn't map neatly onto any Western dessert. "This is super sweet, super salty too at the same time. It's kind of nutty and milky as well. This is super nice," Elizarde says, visibly surprised by the complexity.

"It's a hot day in Amritsar. I'm gonna give the Punjabi kulfi a 10 out of 10, man."

— AJ Elizarde, content creator

What Makes Kulfi Different

For those outside India, kulfi often gets explained as "Indian ice cream," but the comparison undersells the difference. Unlike Western ice cream, which is churned during freezing to incorporate air and achieve a light, fluffy texture, kulfi is made by slowly simmering full-fat milk until it reduces significantly — sometimes to a third of its original volume. The concentrated milk is then sweetened, flavored with cardamom, saffron, pistachios or mango, and frozen in molds without any churning.

The result is dramatically denser and creamier than ice cream, with an almost fudge-like consistency that melts slowly. The slow-cooking process caramelizes the milk sugars, producing a depth of flavor that no amount of vanilla extract can replicate. Street vendors across North India sell it unmolded on sticks, often rolled in crushed pistachios or topped with falooda (thin vermicelli noodles) and rose syrup.

The Comments Section Delivers

The video's comment section became a showcase of kulfi knowledge, with Indian viewers eager to share their regional favorites. "Try the rabdi one kulfi; I am sure you're gonna love it, bro," one user wrote, referring to the version layered with rabdi — a thickened, sweetened milk preparation that adds another dimension of richness. Another noted, "It's pure Punjabi ice cream made with good quality milk," while a third recommended he visit the Golden Temple and try poha — the flattened rice dish popular across central and western India.

One viewer raised a valid question about the "salty" note Elizarde detected: "Wait, why salty? I don't remember kulfi being salty." The answer likely lies in the Punjabi style of kulfi, which sometimes includes a pinch of salt to balance the sweetness — a technique common in many Indian sweets and one that often catches Western palates off guard.

Part of a Bigger Trend

Elizarde's video joins a growing genre of food reaction content from international visitors in India. From Korean tourists trying pani puri to Japanese chefs sampling biryani, these first-taste videos consistently perform well on social media because they offer Indians abroad a vicarious pleasure — watching someone discover flavors they grew up with. For the diaspora, the videos also serve as reminders of the street food experiences that are difficult to replicate overseas, no matter how many Indian grocery stores stock kulfi brands in their freezer aisles.
nri_angle: Kulfi reaction videos resonate with diaspora Indians who miss street food experiences that are difficult to replicate abroad, even with store-bought kulfi brands.
